posts.title: How one team ships to production in five minutes
posts.markdown:
A small finance team we work with deploys dozens of times a day. Most changes start as a draft from an assistant and end as a reviewed pull request with a preview link.

## The loop

1. Open a branch; a preview URL appears within a minute.
2. Reviewers comment on the running page, not the diff alone.
3. Merge, and the change is live everywhere shortly after.

The interesting part is not speed. It is that nobody is afraid of a deploy any more. This is a placeholder customer story.

posts.title: The state of preview deployments
posts.markdown:
Preview deployments started as a convenience and became the place where most review happens. We looked at how teams use them today.

## What we found

Teams that review on previews merge faster and revert less. The previews themselves are short-lived: most are opened a handful of times and never again, which is exactly what you want from a disposable environment.

> A preview is a conversation, not an artefact.

posts.title: Our bug bounty program is now public
posts.markdown:
After a year as an invite-only program, our bug bounty is open to everyone. Researchers can report issues in any of our public services and receive a response within two business days.

## Scope and rewards

- Everything on our primary domains is in scope.
- Rewards scale with impact, not with effort.
- We publish a summary of every fixed issue, with the researcher's permission.

posts.title: Reproducing, disclosing and fixing an image decoder bug
posts.markdown:
A crafted image could make one of our resize workers read past the end of a buffer. Here is how we reproduced it, worked with the upstream maintainers and shipped a fix.

## Timeline

1. Day 0: a fuzzer found a crashing input.
2. Day 1: we confirmed it was reachable and disabled the code path.
3. Day 6: the upstream fix was released and deployed.

No customer data was exposed. Long-form engineering write-ups fit this template's single-column article layout.
posts.excerpt: From a fuzzer crash to an upstream fix in six days.
